items.title: Frankenstein was written by an 18-year-old on a rainy Geneva holiday
items.claim: Mary Shelley conceived Frankenstein in 1816. What were the circumstances?

options.text: She was 18, on a wet summer holiday at Villa Diodati with Byron, Percy Shelley and Polidori, and Byron proposed they each write a ghost story
She was 35, an established novelist commissioned by a London publisher
It was a collaboration with Percy Shelley, who wrote most of it
It started as a science textbook for working men's institutes

items.reveal:
The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora caused 1816 to be the 'year without a summer' across Europe. Mary Godwin (later Shelley), Percy Shelley, Lord Byron, John Polidori and Claire Clairmont were stuck indoors at Villa Diodati on Lake Geneva.

Byron suggested they each write a ghost story. Mary, 18, conceived Frankenstein after a 'waking dream' (her words, in the 1831 preface). Polidori's contribution became 'The Vampyre' (1819), the first English vampire story.

Frankenstein was published anonymously in 1818. Many assumed Percy wrote it; her authorship was credited in the 1823 edition.
items.why: Canonical novels feel inevitable. Frankenstein was an 18-year-old's competition entry — and it founded modern science fiction.

items.title: Dickens was paid by instalment, not by the word
items.claim: Dickens's prose is famously expansive. A persistent myth says he was paid by the word. What was actually the case?

options.text: He was paid by the word, which is why his sentences are long
He was paid per monthly or weekly instalment of serialised fiction — the pressure was to keep readers buying the next issue, not to inflate word count
He was paid only after publication of the complete novel
He was paid a fixed salary by his publisher Chapman and Hall regardless of output

items.reveal:
Most of Dickens's novels were serialised in monthly parts (Pickwick, Dombey, Bleak House) or weekly (Hard Times, Great Expectations). He typically agreed an advance per instalment, with profit-sharing or royalty arrangements that varied by contract.

The 'paid by the word' myth seems to come from confusing serial pay (which incentivises cliffhangers, recurring characters and emotional hooks) with line-rate journalism. Wilkie Collins, Trollope and Hardy used similar serial structures.

Dickens's prose style — its rhythm, its returning motifs, its cliffhangers — is shaped by serial form, not by an imagined per-word cheque.
items.why: Misremembered economic incentives make literary criticism sloppy. The actual incentive (keep them buying next month) explains form better than the fake one (pad the sentence).

items.title: The novel as a form is only about 300 years old in English
items.claim: Tragedy, epic poetry and lyric are ancient. When did the English novel emerge as a recognisable form?

options.text: Around 1700 BCE, with the Epic of Gilgamesh
In the late 17th and early 18th centuries — Aphra Behn's Oroonoko (1688), Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719), Richardson's Pamela (1740)
With Chaucer's Canterbury Tales in the 14th century

items.reveal:
Ian Watt's 'The Rise of the Novel' (1957) traced the English novel to Defoe, Richardson and Fielding, linking it to the rise of the middle class, print capitalism and Protestant interiority. Earlier prose narratives existed (Don Quixote, 1605; Genji, 11th century) but the realist, character-centred novel in English coalesces around 1700-1750.

The Greek and Latin canons had long prose works (Petronius's Satyricon, Heliodorus's Aethiopica) but these are episodic and rhetorical, not novelistic in Watt's sense.

Novels were initially considered a low, suspect form — read by women, dangerous to morals.
items.why: Treating 'literature' as a timeless category hides the fact that the novel itself is a modernity-shaped form. Its conventions (free indirect discourse, the omniscient narrator, the bildungsroman) emerged with the bourgeoisie.
